name: Composio Remote Sandbox (COMPOSIO_REMOTE_WORKBENCH)
engine: Hosted "persistent Jupyter notebook" per session on Composio's infrastructure (standard tier 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM); engine and isolation technology not stated.
how_run: Not run: the remote sandbox is reached through a Composio session (COMPOSIO_API_KEY), and the experimental local sandbox also needs a session and injects COMPOSIO_API_KEY into the sandbox. No credentials were used.

source_notes.finding: Helper functions pre-initialized in the notebook: run_composio_tool (any Composio tool by slug), invoke_llm, upload_local_file, proxy_execute, web_search, smart_file_extract.
Meta tools: SEARCH_TOOLS finds tools, MULTI_EXECUTE runs simple calls, COMPOSIO_REMOTE_WORKBENCH runs code for bulk or multi-step work.
run_composio_tool calls back to Composio's Tool Router, which holds the user's connected-account auth. In the local variant every call routes back through the Tool Router.

Not stated for the remote sandbox. For the local sandbox the docs say "The sandbox is your security boundary" and that the project COMPOSIO_API_KEY is injected into the sandbox env, readable by any code and acting across every connection on the project.
Not documented beyond notebook execution results and files on the /mnt/files mount.
Compute tiers only (1 vCPU / 1 GB default). No time or output limits documented.
Persistent Jupyter notebook per session; /mnt/files survives sandbox restarts.
The sandbox "corrects common mistakes in the code your agent generates", for example mapping result["apiKey"] to api_key instead of failing.
Packages not preinstalled are installed automatically on use. invoke_llm inside the sandbox is the only Composio-side LLM usage. Sandboxes are not billed today.

surprises: The sandbox silently rewrites failing code ("resolves the mismatch instead of failing"), so the model can get results from code that would have errored.
The local sandbox puts the project-wide COMPOSIO_API_KEY inside the sandbox environment, where any model-written code can read it.
Missing packages are installed automatically, which implies outbound package-index access from the sandbox (inferred, not tested).
